sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe correct error-correction procedures that preserve the original entry and require initials and date.
- Explain amendments and late entries, including the patient's right to request amendment and the rules for clearly labeled, dated late entries.
- Recognize the importance of audit trails for accountability, security, and record integrity.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Fixing a mistake is like crossing out a wrong answer on homework with one line and writing the right answer next to it—you keep the old one visible so everyone can see what changed.

### Question 2

Think of a record like a diary of care. If you scribble out a page so no one can read it, later readers can't tell what really happened.

### Question 3

White-out is like painting over a road sign—drivers can't see the real message underneath. A record must stay readable.

### Question 4

Signing and dating a correction is like signing your name on a school paper—it shows who did the work and when.

### Question 5

A late entry is like adding a note to your homework after you handed it in—you must say when you're adding it so it isn't mistaken for the original work.

### Question 6

It's like putting a 'sent later' stamp on a note so no one thinks you wrote it on the original day.

### Question 7

The computer keeps a little automatic diary of who opened or changed each file and when—no one has to write it down.

### Question 8

An audit trail is like a security camera log for files—it records who was there and what they did.

### Question 9

If your report card has a mistake, you can ask the school to fix it—but you don't get to fill it in yourself.

### Question 10

A routine correction fixes a typo you made; an amendment is a formal request to change what the record says about someone.

### Question 11

The person who wrote the note knows best what it should say—like the author of a story fixing their own sentence.

### Question 12

If you see a mistake in someone else's important work, you tell them instead of fixing it yourself without permission.

### Question 13

The computer's 'fix' button keeps a copy of the old words and notes what you changed—like a save-history for your document.

### Question 14

A medical record is like a time capsule of someone's care—you keep it honest so the future can trust it.

### Question 15

Putting your name and the date on a change is like signing a permission slip—it shows who approved it and when.

### Question 16

If a fact about you is wrong, you ask the office through their official form—you don't grab the pen yourself.

### Question 17

The audit trail is like a sign-in sheet plus a change log: who, what, and when.

### Question 18

Backdating is like putting yesterday's date on today's homework—it makes people think you did it earlier than you did.

### Question 19

A late entry needs two time stamps: when the thing happened and when you wrote about it.

### Question 20

White-out hides the original words forever, like painting over a clue in a mystery.

### Question 21

A medical record is like an official scorecard—it has to be clear and honest because people may rely on it later.

### Question 22

Fix your typo in someone's address the proper way—cross it out, write the right one, and sign and date it.

### Question 23

The date is like a time stamp on a photo—it tells you when something happened.

### Question 24

The amendment right covers the 'official files' the office actually uses to make decisions about you.

### Question 25

When you're not sure of the rule, ask an adult in charge—don't just guess.

### Question 26

If a doctor wrote the wrong date, tell the doctor—don't erase their note yourself.

### Question 27

You can ask the office to review what's written, but no one should secretly erase a doctor's finding.

### Question 28

If you forgot to write something down, you add it later and clearly say 'I'm adding this now.'

### Question 29

If a teammate is doing something that could hurt patients, tell the coach—don't join in.

### Question 30

When something goes wrong, the computer's log shows who was there—like a security camera replay.

### Question 31

There's a proper office process for deciding, and the assistant follows it rather than deciding on the spot.

### Question 32

The person who wrote the note knows what it was supposed to say, so they are the right one to fix it.

### Question 33

Put the added note where the story of the visit lives, but label it 'added later' with today's date.

### Question 34

An addendum is like attaching a sticky note to a page instead of scribbling over the page.

### Question 35

If someone asks you to change work that isn't yours and that they can't verify, say no and send it to the right person.

### Question 36

Records must stay true because doctors, courts, and auditors all rely on what they say.

### Question 37

If a test result lands in the wrong file, you have to fix the wrong file and tell the team—hiding it is dangerous.

### Question 38

The audit trail makes sure every change leaves a footprint, so sneaky edits can be spotted.

### Question 39

The computer keeps a log of who looked at a file, so the office can check it when needed.

### Question 40

The person who adds the note signs it, like signing your name to work you turned in.

### Question 41

Cross out the wrong number with one line, write the right number, and sign and date it.

### Question 42

Saying why you're late with the note is like explaining a late homework so the teacher understands.

### Question 43

If the office won't change it, you can add your own note saying 'I disagree' that stays with the record.

### Question 44

The right to ask for a fix is real, but it doesn't let you demand the record be rewritten to your liking.

### Question 45

No one should 'tidy' a record by hiding the truth—that's like erasing a mistake in the rulebook.

### Question 46

The fix is attached right next to the original so the full story stays together.

### Question 47

The computer's security camera should stay on; you don't unplug it to save battery.

### Question 48

Only the person who wrote it, or someone the office officially allows, should change a record.

### Question 49

If the doctor isn't there, mark the problem and wait—don't rewrite the doctor's words yourself.

### Question 50

The log shows exactly what happened, which can clear an honest person just as easily as catch a dishonest one.

### Question 51

Updating an address is a normal, permitted fix—just do it the right way and note the change.

### Question 52

Fixing your phone number is a quick office update; changing what a doctor wrote goes through a formal review.

### Question 53

Show the old and the new, side by side, with your initials and the date—like a before-and-after with a signature.

### Question 54

The office can say no only for specific fair reasons, like the info being correct already.

### Question 55

Use the 'fix with a note' button, not the trash can, when correcting a record.

### Question 56

An added-later note is fine if it honestly says when it was added and what it refers to.

### Question 57

To explain what happened to a file, check the computer's log—don't guess.

### Question 58

Signing and dating a change is like putting your name on a receipt—it shows who did it and when.

### Question 59

If a contact number is out of date, update it the proper way and note the change.

### Question 60

Attribution means signing your work so everyone knows who did what.

### Question 61

Fix the typo right away using the proper method—one line, the right word, your initials, and the date.

### Question 62

Keep the original readable so anyone can see the 'before' and 'after' clearly.

### Question 63

Write the note now, label it 'added later,' and include both the call time and the time you're writing it.

### Question 64

The system automatically keeps a log of who did what—that's the audit trail.

### Question 65

Fix the wrong number the right way and note the change, so billing goes to the right place.

### Question 66

The designated record set is the official collection of files the office actually uses to make decisions about you.

### Question 67

Erasing so no one can tell is like hiding evidence—it's not allowed, even for small mistakes.

### Question 68

Hiding the original is the dangerous one—the others keep everything visible and signed.

### Question 69

Stay calm, explain the official way to request a change, and get help—don't delete anything.

### Question 70

A change with no name is like a mystery edit—no one knows who did it or if it was allowed.

### Question 71

A wrong-file lab result is urgent—tell the medical team right away, then fix the paperwork.

### Question 72

The log catches people peeking at files they have no work reason to open.

### Question 73

If the office says no, you can still add your own 'I disagree' note that stays in the file.

### Question 74

Faking the date is what ruins a late entry—honesty about timing is the whole point.

### Question 75

You can't rewrite what happened just to help a claim get paid—that's not what records are for.

### Question 76

A correction is fixing your own typo; an amendment is a formal request to change what the record says.

### Question 77

When you're not sure you're allowed to change something, ask the person in charge instead of acting.

### Question 78

Just peeking at a file counts, even if you don't change anything—the log still shows it.

### Question 79

After a fix is made, the corrected version should show up in what the patient gets.

### Question 80

A late entry is for whole pieces of information that were missing; a correction is for quick fixes.

### Question 81

Fix the file with the tool that leaves a note about the change—don't silently erase or turn off the camera.

### Question 82

A camera log plus clear rules is the best defense against tampering.

### Question 83

Allergies are safety-critical—don't delete them; bring the request to the medical team.

### Question 84

Keep both the old page and the correction note so the full story stays clear.

### Question 85

Doing documentation the right way keeps patients safe and keeps the office honest—it's not just paperwork.
